sentences.text: Vallibonavenatrix was a moderately sized bipedal predator belonging to the spinosaurid family.
Its back featured moderately tall dorsal neural spines, with one expanded into a trapezoidal, fan-like shape similar to Ichthyovenator, suggesting a sail-like structure.
The skeleton included a sacrum and ilium containing deep depressions and air-filled pneumatic openings, indicating lightweight bone structure.
This specimen represents the most complete spinosaurid fossil discovered on the Iberian Peninsula.
Elisabete Malafaia and colleagues formally described the species Vallibonavenatrix cani in 2019 based on a partial skeleton.
The generic name Vallibonavenatrix combines the town of Vallibona with the Latin word for huntress.
The specific name 'cani' honors Juan Cano Forner, the amateur fossil collector who discovered the remains.

In 2019, Malafaia and colleagues classified Vallibonavenatrix within the family Spinosauridae, a group of large-bodied tetanuran dinosaurs traditionally divided into two subfamilies, Spinosaurinae and Baryonychinae.

Based on their analysis, Malafaia and colleagues found Vallibonavenatrix more closely related to spinosaurines like Spinosaurus and Irritator than to baryonychines like Baryonyx, placing it within the subfamily Spinosaurinae.
Certain anatomical characteristics suggest Vallibonavenatrix may have an affinity with spinosaurines rather than baryonychines.

However, a 2021 study by Chris Barker and colleagues found Vallibonavenatrix's phylogenetic position unstable, placing it either as the most basal spinosaurid outside both subfamilies or within Baryonychinae depending on the analysis method.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Vallibonavenatrix as Baryonychinae.
A 2025 reassessment by Rauhut and colleagues recovered Vallibonavenatrix within Spinosaurinae, diverging after Iberospinus.
Vallibonavenatrix lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 129.4 and 125 million years ago.
It shared its environment with Iguanodon bernissartensis, Morelladon beltrani, an indeterminate sauropod, and the spinosaurid Protathlitis.
